summary:
Climate on farms is changing faster than farmers can notice, yet most still decide what to sow based on habit. CropOrbit turns NASA data from orbit into a clear plan for one specific field.

It takes three steps. The farmer finds their field by parcel number or on the map, adds the crops they grew in recent years and sets their priorities, such as water, soil or income. In seconds, CropOrbit analyses decades of NASA climate, terrain and vegetation data together with soil information. It scores 20 crops for that exact field, tests thousands of possible rotations and puts the farmer’s current plan side by side with the 3 best alternatives. A year calendar shows when frost, drought, heat or bare soil put the field at risk. Each recommendation explains why it works, what the risks are and how certain the data is, and ends in a printable report.

CropOrbit supports farmers and advisors, it does not replace them. From orbit to your field.
details:
What it does and how it works
CropOrbit is a web app that recommends a better crop rotation for one specific field. The farmer works through three steps. First, they find the field by parcel number, by searching a village or by clicking or drawing it on the map. Second, they add the crops grown in the last 2–6 years, or mark it as a new field. Third, they describe the farm (irrigation, livestock, cover crops, straw) and set 7 priority sliders. One click on “Analyse field” fetches the data and shows results in 5 tabs: Conditions, Crops, Rotations, Calendar and Report.

CropOrbit scores 20 crops from 0 to 100 using the law of the minimum, where the weakest factor decides. A rotation generator tests thousands of variants that follow agronomic rules and rates each on 7 axes (water, soil, erosion, nitrogen, disease, income and feed), weighted by the farmer’s priorities. The current rotation is shown next to the 3 best alternatives.

Where NASA data powers the app

  • Step 1, finding the field: NASA SRTM (30 m terrain) gives the field’s elevation, slope and aspect. Elevation corrects NASA POWER temperatures to the field’s real height.
  • Conditions tab: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and CERES, 24 years of daily data) drives the tiles for growing season, frost, water balance, soil drought and heat, plus the trend charts.
  • Crops tab: NASA POWER provides the heat, water, winter survival, frost and heat factors in each crop’s score. SRTM slope limits row crops such as maize on steep fields.
  • Rotations tab: NASA POWER feeds the water axis (FAO-56 evaporation and crop water deficit) and rainfall erosivity. SRTM slope gives the LS factor in the RUSLE erosion model.
  • Calendar tab: NASA POWER marks frost, drought, heat and heavy rain across the year. NASA MODIS NDVI (250 m satellite greenness) confirms when the soil is bare.
  • Report tab: every value shows its NASA source and confidence level.

Benefits and impact
Farmers get field-level climate insight that was only available to researchers before. Better rotations mean less bare soil, less erosion, more organic matter and lower drought risk. The app lists data gaps and points to check with an advisor, and ends with a printable report. CropOrbit supports farmers and advisors, it does not replace them.

Tools and technology

  • Backend: Python 3, standard library only
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a framework, Leaflet maps and Chart.js charts
  • Data: NASA POWER, NASA SRTM, NASA MODIS, ISRIC SoilGrids, the Polish land registry (GUGiK ULDK and EGiB), USDA FoodData Central and GUS
  • Methods: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith, FAO Ecocrop/GAEZ, RUSLE and VDLUFA humus balance
  • Hosting: GitHub Codespaces with on-disk caching
  • Bilingual EN/PL interface, mobile-friendly and WCAG 2.1 AA accessible

Creativity
CropOrbit compares whole multi-year rotations, not single crops, and links global NASA data with local land registry soil classes down to a single parcel. All explanations are generated from calculated numbers, so nothing is said that cannot be traced back to the data.

Factors we considered
We designed the app for farmers who are not computer experts, so it has a simple 3-step flow, plain language and two languages. We state limitations openly: NASA POWER has about 50 km resolution, soil moisture is modelled and SoilGrids is a 250 m model. We show trade-offs honestly, for example when a rotation saves soil but uses slightly more water. Next steps are NASA SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, ECOSTRESS heat stress, local yields and prices, and calibration with agricultural advisors.
